L148: ##
L149: ## Abstract
L150: 
L151:     Cryptoasset systems often bind cryptographic key control to financial control: losing a wallet seed, custody share, hardware device, or smart-account credential can remove spend authority, while compromised recovery can enable theft. Existing work treats recovery through separate vocabularies-key backup, secret sharing, account recovery, credential re-issuance, social recovery, and asset migration-making mechanisms and tradeoffs difficult to compare.
L152:     This paper presents a Systematization of Knowledge (SoK) on cryptographic key recovery for cryptoasset custody and financial technologies.
L153: Starting from a 118-paper systematic-review discovery corpus, we derive a 77-paper synthesis corpus and code each retained system in a master matrix covering recovered objects, recovery semantics, mechanisms, enrollment and storage, authorization, trust placement, failure events, post-recovery state, validation evidence, deployment status, privacy, usability, and limitations.
L154: The matrix supports an axis-first taxonomy that separates secret-restoring, hybrid, control-restoring, forensic/extractive, and framework-oriented recovery.
L155:     Our central observation is that recovery is not a single operation: systems may reconstruct an original secret, regenerate a seed, restore a share, reissue a credential, migrate signing authority, restore account control, move assets, or extract forensic artifacts.
L156: We derive a generalized construction model, check it against production-facing designs, and identify six findings: recovery semantics are heterogeneous; recovery shifts trust; liveness improvements create abuse paths; post-recovery lifecycle management is uneven; protocol evidence outpaces user evidence; and recovery metadata remains underprotected. These gaps motivate a research agenda for recovery-aware financial technologies.

L18: # Signed Permissions and Action Receipts for Automated Agents
L19: ## 【0†Abstract】
L20: This document specifies records with which a third party can establish, later and without network access, what an automated agent, such as an artificial intelligence (AI) agent, was permitted to do and what it recorded doing. The person for whom the agent acts, the principal, signs a permission with a passkey; the permission carries limits that a verifier can check mechanically. The agent signs a receipt for each action with Ed25519 and the Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm (ML-DSA-87).
L21: Receipts are chained and entered in a log whose signed tree heads are time-stamped. A verifier reports, separately, whether the records are sound and whether each recorded action stayed within its permission. The content of each record is specified independently of its encoding; one encoding, JSON Web Signature (JWS) over canonical JavaScript Object Notation (JSON), is defined.【1†¶】

L133: ## 【23†1.】 【24†Introduction】
L134: A principal signs a permission for an agent: which actions, with which services, within which limits, from when until when. The agent signs a receipt for each action it takes; a service may countersign it. A recorder appends receipts to a log and periodically signs its tree head, which a Time-Stamping Authority (TSA) time-stamps.
L135: Later, with no network access, a verifier checks the records and answers three separate questions: whether the records are sound, whether every signature could be verified on that device, and whether each recorded action stayed within its permission.【115†¶】
L136: This document specifies the records and the verifier's rules: evidence, not enforcement. Nothing in this document stops an action when it is attempted, and an action for which no receipt was written leaves no trace in the agent's own log (【6†Section 18】).
L137: It names the role of an enforcement point that refuses an action before it takes effect, an executor (【5†Section 2】), but does not specify how an executor decides or keeps its records, how records are carried, how keys and trust anchors are distributed, or what to do about a finding (【116†Section 15】).【117†¶】
L138: When an automated agent acts for a person, the questions asked afterward are the same: was the action authorized, by whom, within what limits, did the other party agree, and when? Authorization protocols answer at the moment of a request, typically with tokens that are not kept as evidence. This document specifies records that a third party can verify later, without network access. Each record is signed by the party that made it.
L139: Whoever keeps the log can still leave out or delay entries; 【6†Section 18】 states how far that reaches.【118†¶】

L146: ## Abstract
L147: 
L148: Agentic AI systems are increasingly capable of autonomous decision-making and collaboration across distributed environments. However, existing frameworks largely assume trust among agents, without providing mechanisms for verifiable identity, behavioral accountability, or interaction transparency.
L149: This work proposes a blockchain-based backbone infrastructure that enables a verifiable trust layer for autonomous multi-agent systems. Agent identities are bound to decentralized identifiers (DIDs) registered on-chain, while an on-chain Agent Registry enables reputation-aware capability discovery.
L150: By integrating smart contracts, DIDs, and verifiable credentials (VCs), the framework ensures that trust is not assumed but earned through interactions: agents issue VC endorsements after each task, and dedicated smart contracts automatically update reputation scores, applying incentives and penalties accordingly.
L151: Blockchain provides immutability, transparency, and programmability, transforming trust from an implicit assumption into an explicit, auditable, and enforceable property of the multi-agent ecosystem.
L152: ## INTRODUCTION
L153: Agentic Artificial Intelligence (Agentic AI) systems represent a significant evolution in the design of autonomous computational entities. Unlike traditional large language model (LLM) applications that operate in a simple prompt-response paradigm, agentic systems are capable of planning, tool invocation, delegation, and interagent coordination (Yao et al. 【21†2022】; Yang et al. 【22†2023】).
L154: These capabilities enable the construction of distributed multi-agent ecosystems in which autonomous agents collaborate to accomplish complex tasks.
L155: However, as autonomy and interconnectivity increase, the problem of trust becomes central. In existing agentic frameworks, trust relationships are typically implicit: agents rely on declarative metadata, configuration-level assumptions, or local policies to determine whether another agent is trustworthy (Anthropic 【23†2024】; Google 【24†2025b】).
L156: There is generally no cryptographic guarantee that an agent's declared identity corresponds to its operational instance, nor is there an immutable mechanism for verifying authorization or recording accountability. This implicit trust model introduces systemic vulnerabilities. Malicious or compromised agents may misrepresent capabilities, impersonate other agents, or execute unauthorized actions without a verifiable audit trail.
L157: As agentic systems are increasingly deployed in distributed and potentially adversarial environments, the absence of a formalized trust infrastructure becomes a critical limitation.
L158: In this work, we propose a blockchain-based backbone infrastructure for enabling trustworthy Agentic AI. By externalizing identity provisioning, reputation management, and interaction endorsement to a public decentralized ledger (Nakamoto 【25†2008】), we transform trust from an implicit assumption into a programmatically enforceable and auditable system property. Our architecture integrates decentralized identifiers (DIDs) (Sporny et al. 【26†2022】), verifiable credentials (VCs) (Sporny et al.
L159: 【27†2022】), and smart contracts (Wood 【28†2014】) to establish a verifiable trust layer that operates independently from agent logic.
L160: The contribution of this work lies in the design and proof-of-concept implementation of a hybrid off-chain/on-chain architecture that: (i) binds agent identities to blockchain-anchored DIDs provisioned by authorized operators; (ii) enables reputation-aware capability discovery and credential verification prior to delegation; and (iii) supports interaction-driven trust evolution through verifiable endorsements.
L161: The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section “Background” provides background on agentic AI, blockchain as a trust anchor, and decentralized identity standards. Section “Related work” reviews related work. Section “Architecture” presents the proposed architecture. Section “Implementation” describes the implementation. Section “Conclusion” concludes the paper and outlines future work.
